title: Functions, recursion and structures
subtitle: Break a big problem into named pieces, and group related data into one unit.

sections.title: Defining and calling functions
sections.body: A function has a return type, name, parameters and body: int square(int x) { return x * x; }. Declare a prototype before use so the compiler knows the signature. void functions return nothing. Benefits: reuse, testing one piece at a time, readability.

questions.prompt: A function prototype tells the compiler…

choices.text: The name, parameter types and return type.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: So calls can be checked before the body is seen.

sections.title: Scope and lifetime
sections.body: Local variables live inside a function (or block) and vanish when it returns; each call has its own copy. Global variables are visible everywhere but make code harder to reason about. static locals keep their value between calls.

questions.prompt: Two different functions each declare int i. They are…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Locals are private to their function.

sections.title: The call stack
sections.body: Each call pushes a stack frame holding parameters, locals and the return address; return pops it. Recursion simply stacks many frames.

choices.text: A base case that stops the calls.

figures.caption: Figure 7.3.1 — The call stack
figures.note: Five nested frames build up, then unwind multiplying.

sections.title: Recursion vs iteration
sections.body: Anything recursive can be written with a loop. Recursion is natural for trees and divide-and-conquer; iteration is cheaper (no frames). The naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes subproblems: fib(6) makes 25 calls.

questions.prompt: Why is iteration usually cheaper than recursion?

figures.note: Step through to see the overlapping calls.

sections.title: Structures
sections.body: A struct bundles fields of different types: struct Student { int roll; int marks; };. Access with the dot operator (s.marks), or arrow through a pointer (p->marks). Assigning one struct to another copies every field.

worked.why: struct { char c; int i; } on a typical machine: c takes 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding so i is 4-aligned.

sections.title: Arrays of structs, unions, enums
sections.body: An array of structs models a table (students). A union shares one memory slot between its members (size = largest member). enum gives names to integer constants (enum {RED, GREEN, BLUE}; = 0, 1, 2). typedef creates a shorter type name.

questions.prompt: A union of an int (4 B) and a double (8 B) occupies…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Members overlap; size is the largest.
